title: Quantitative analysis of HDAC inhibition using the TGx-HDACi transcriptomic biomarker in human TK6 cells
abstract: Transcriptomic biomarkers provide an objective approach for extracting mechanistic information from complex gene expression datasets and may support quantitative applications in chemical assessment. TGx-HDACi is an 81-gene transcriptomic biomarker designed to identify histone deacetylase inhibitors (HDACi) in human TK6 cells. We evaluated whether benchmark concentrations (BMCs) derived from TGx-HDACi responses are concordant with BMCs based on reductions in HDAC enzyme activity. Human TK6 cells were exposed to concentration ranges of three HDAC inhibitors from different representative classes: the pan-HDAC inhibitors trichostatin A (TSA) and valproic acid (VPA), and the class I-selective inhibitor entinostat. HDAC enzyme activity and TGx-HDACi responses were assessed, and concentration-response modeling was performed to derive BMCs. TGx-HDACi correctly identified all three compounds as HDAC inhibitors and showed concentration-dependent responses. For TSA and VPA, TGx-HDACi and HDAC activity BMCs had overlapping confidence intervals, indicating good agreement between potency measures. In contrast, entinostat produced higher TGx-HDACi BMCs than the enzyme assay. This reduced quantitative concordance may reflect differences in HDAC selectivity, as TGx-HDACi was developed primarily using pan-HDAC inhibitors and appears less responsive to the more limited transcriptional changes induced by class I-selective inhibitors. Overall, these results demonstrate that TGx-HDACi reliably identifies HDAC inhibition and can provide potency estimates that align with enzyme activity measures for some HDAC inhibitor classes. However, the findings highlight the importance of considering biomarker applicability domain when interpreting potency estimates across compounds with differing HDAC selectivity.

title: Comparative Profiling of Cytosolic Accumulation of Cell-Penetrating Peptides in Mammalian and Bacterial Cells
abstract: Delivering molecules to the cytosol remains a major bottleneck in antibacterial therapy, as both the Gram-negative bacterial envelope and host-cell membranes restrict intracellular access. Cell-penetrating peptides (CPPs) offer a potential strategy for overcoming these barriers. However, selecting CPPs for conjugate development remains largely empirical, in part because conventional fluorescence-based uptake measurements can misidnentify cellular association as cytosolic delivery.

title: N-terminal mutations R5L and R5H share a common mechanism in disrupting tau condensates on microtubule surfaces
abstract: Tau, an intrinsically disordered protein abundant in neuronal axons, forms cooperative condensates on microtubule (MT) surfaces that regulate motor proteins and protect MTs from severing enzymes. Disease-associated mutations at residue 5 in the N-terminal projection domain of tau, far from the MT-tau binding interface, have been linked to progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP) (R5L) and frontotemporal dementia (FTD) (R5H). While R5L was previously shown to disrupt tau condensate formation on MT surfaces, it remained unclear whether R5H shares this phenotype. Using total internal reflection fluorescence (TIRF) microscopy, we show that both mutations reduce condensate packing density compared to WT tau under sub-saturating conditions at physiological pH (7.4), indicating impaired tau-tau cooperativity despite their distal location from the MT-tau binding interface. Single-molecule measurements further show both the dwell time and landing rate of tau within condensates are reduced while behavior on bare MTs remains unchanged, implicating weakened tau-tau cooperativity rather than disrupted binding to MTs. Strikingly, mutational analysis identifies the positive charge at residue 5 as critical for tau condensate formation: the charge-preserving R5K substitution retains WT-like behavior, whereas the charge-eliminating R5I substitution behaves like R5H/R5L. Further supporting this mechanism, R5H exhibits a pronounced pH dependence, transitioning from WT-like behavior at pH 6.4 to R5L-like behavior at pH 7.4 upon histidine deprotonation. Together, these findings establish that the positive charge at R5 is critical for tau condensate formation on MT surfaces and identify a common mechanism linking PSP and FTD.

title: Multimodal conformational landscape and thermodynamics of coupled folding and binding in an intrinsically disordered protein region
abstract: Intrinsically disordered proteins and peptides, as well as flexible protein regions, often bind folded protein partners through coupled folding and binding, but the underlying conformational landscapes and thermodynamics remain challenging to resolve. The large conformational space of the unbound molecule and its interactions with the folded partner make it difficult to identify and efficiently sample the slow collective motions governing association and folding. Here, we use enhanced-sampling molecular dynamics to investigate the coupled binding and folding of the intrinsically disordered region of FCP1 phosphatase upon interaction with the folded transcription factor Rap74, a process that modulates the activity of RNA polymerase II. OneOPES enhanced sampling simulations reveal a multimodal binding landscape comprising native, flipped and disordered-bound states, and identify hydrophobic contacts as early determinants of association followed by progressive helix formation. Circuit topology analysis further elucidates the FCP1 folding mechanism by identifying a characteristic topological transition accompanying helix formation and its stabilisation upon binding. To resolve the thermodynamics of the process, we introduce Divide et impera, a thermodynamic decomposition that separates the free-energy cost of folding from the binding free energy of the folded conformation. This approach reduces the conformational complexity of individual calculations while preserving the thermodynamic connection between unbound and bound states, enabling the calculation of absolute binding free energies in close agreement with experiment. These results establish a framework for connecting conformational heterogeneity, binding mechanisms and thermodynamics in coupled folding and binding of disordered proteins, with potential applications in the rational design and development of peptide therapeutics.

title: Tailoring CeOx/Cu Synergistic Interface for Ampere-Level CO2-to-Ethanol Conversion via Cu Penetration Electrode
abstract: The adsorption of the *CO intermediate and the dissociation of H2O are of crucial significance for synergistically facilitating *CO intermediate hydrogenation and thereby triggering *CO–*CHO asymmetric C–C coupling during CO2 electroreduction. However, achieving the controllable construction of synergistic active sites and their quantitative characterization remains challenging.

title: Controlling the flow of information in optical metrology
abstract: Optical metrology has surpassed the Abbe–Rayleigh limit by leveraging nonlinear phenomena and statistical accumulation, and has recently unlocked subatomic precision using artificial intelligence estimators trained on measurand variations. Here we argue that further gains can be achieved by optimizing the flow of Fisher information carrying metrological content. We show that Fisher information flow need not follow the optical energy flow and that it exhibits resonance, diffraction and interference, singular points, and vorticity. It can exhibit a Talbot-like effect in which Fisher information density patterns repeat periodically with propagation distance, and it can be focused beyond the diffraction limit, mirroring the effect of optical superoscillation. Material composition, resonances, geometry and environment determine where information is generated, how it propagates, and how it can be enhanced and directed to improve precision. This perspective recasts metrology as information flow engineering, for applications ranging from atomic-scale diagnostics and smart manufacturing to remote sensing, radar and LiDAR.

title: Variationally correct physics-informed operator learning for nonlinear partial differential equations
abstract: Physics-informed operator learning trains neural operators on the residual of a parametric partial differential equation (PDE) instead of labeled solution data, but its reliability depends on a variationally correct residual: one that is equivalent to the error in a norm dictated by the equation, the PDE-compliant norm. For nonlinear equations written as first-order systems, we prove that the first-order system least-squares residual is equivalent to the error in this norm near a solution branch if the linearized residual is stable and the residual derivative is Lipschitz continuous, possibly in a norm stronger than the error norm. We verify these conditions for monotone reaction, solution- and gradient-dependent diffusion, and compressible Neo-Hookean hyperelasticity. The stability mechanisms vary across these classes, as do the regions where the equivalence holds, from arbitrary bounded sets to a neighborhood of the branch. In a conforming finite element space, we show that the loss excess of a state near the finite element solution is equivalent to its squared distance from that solution. We use this loss to train a reduced basis neural operator with values in this space, with solution snapshots needed only for the basis and the loss and its symbolically derived gradient assembled by the finite element library. At inference, this loss estimates the error. Numerically, the square root of the loss excess tracks the error within factors comparable to those of the linear case, and the operator achieves higher accuracy in the PDE-compliant norm than grid-based baselines evaluated in the same finite element space.

title: Generative AI and the Crisis of Higher Education Assessments: Examining 'AI-Proofing' Strategies for College-Level Assessments
abstract: Higher education is confronting an academic-integrity challenge unlike any in its history. Students can now outsource homework, take-home assignments, and online examinations to large language models (LLMs) that complete them in seconds. Existing research on evaluating LLM performance on academic assessments has focused largely on standardized examinations, or on questions from college-level courses drawn from a single discipline. Far less is known about how LLMs perform on college-level assessment questions spanning multiple disciplines, that instructors have purposely designed to be AI-resistant, and about which features of such questions, if any, meaningfully constrain LLM performance. We address this gap by collecting 75 questions from authentic college coursework assessments, spanning 17 disciplines, which were contributed by 37 faculty members from ten U.S. universities and one U.K. university. Of these, 61 questions were intentionally designed by faculty members to be 'LLM-proof', while the remaining 14 questions were sourced from online courses. We then (i) evaluate three state-of-the-art LLMs' ability to correctly answer these questions with and without supplementary course materials; (ii) identify five strategies, through thematic analysis, that faculty used to make their questions harder for LLMs to solve; and (iii) test whether these strategies impact LLMs' ability to answer the questions accurately. Our experimental results show that the best-performing model scored approximately 83% without supplementary course materials and 85% with them, and we observed noteworthy differences across models, answer formats, and instructor tweaking strategies. We discuss implications for assessment design, academic-integrity policy, and the broader ethics of deploying LLMs in educational settings.

title: Emergent Steering Beyond Endpoint Alignment in Chemical Reaction Models
abstract: Machine learning models for chemical reaction prediction are usually evaluated by endpoint accuracy, but endpoint correctness alone does not reveal how a model represents chemical transformation or why it fails. We introduce UniRxnAxis, a unified forward-retrosynthesis framework that models both tasks as direction-conditioned endpoint redistribution in a shared latent space. By aligning source states, transformed states, and encoded target endpoints, UniRxnAxis enables directional auditing of learned latent updates. This shared latent geometry allows the learned displacement (from the encoder source state $S_0$ to the decoder-facing transformed state $S_1$) to be decomposed into an endpoint-parallel component and an endpoint-orthogonal residual, which we call emergent steering. Our evaluation shows that emergent steering is functionally important: in retrosynthesis, it recovers most of the model's utility, remains effective under random, shuffled, and prototype controls, and directly affects which bond edits are promoted or suppressed. The residual-over-parallel ordering persists across alignment strengths, after decoder-interface calibration, against angle-matched random axes, and in a second graph-edit architecture, although its magnitude depends on the reference axis and optimization. The decomposition also supports a proxy taxonomy of model-side failures, showing how reaction models can be audited beyond endpoint accuracy.

title: Variational Monte Carlo for Quantum Excited States via Nested Low-Rank Approximation
abstract: The electronic Schrödinger equation encodes a molecule's electronic structure and quantum properties, but solving it scales exponentially with the number of electrons. Solving this equation with neural-network variational Monte Carlo (VMC) has reached chemical accuracy on the ground state of small molecules; extending this success to excited states is constrained by two existing paradigms. Penalty-based methods need $K$ Laplacians per step but require tuning the overlap-penalty weights against the energy gaps they aim to compute. Natural excited states VMC (NES-VMC) is penalty-free, but it combines the $K$ ansatzes into one determinant, whose local energy requires $K^2$ Laplacians per step. We resolve this trade-off via low-rank approximation (LoRA) reparameterization of the rank-$K$ variational objective. The reparameterized objective admits a VMC-compatible stochastic gradient estimator via MCMC sampling from the per-state Born densities, and a sequential nesting scheme recovers the lowest $K$ eigenstates in eigenvalue order. The resulting algorithm, NestedLoRA-VMC, inherits a global optimality guarantee from the LoRA principle. On the first-row atoms Li through Ne at $K=10$, its accuracy is comparable to that of NES-VMC and of a state-of-the-art penalty-based method.

title: Variational and geometric time-dependent density-functional theory of electronic systems
abstract: A central problem in time-dependent density-functional theory (TDDFT) is to construct a time-dependent many-electron wave function that reproduces a prescribed time-dependent electron density. This problem admits a natural geometric interpretation, which in turn leads to at least two distinct formulations of TDDFT. The first is the usual variational formulation of TDDFT, in which the density constraint is enforced with a real-valued local potential. The second is geometric TDDFT, introduced in recent works, in which the same density constraint is enforced with an imaginary local potential, or equivalently with a Hermitian nonlocal potential. In this work, we develop this unified viewpoint for continuous electronic systems and systematically compare the two formulations. We formulate the corresponding time-dependent Kohn-Sham schemes and derive a number of exact conditions for geometric TDDFT, including conditions associated with causality, time-reversal symmetry, uniform-coordinate scaling, translational invariance, energy and momentum equations of motion, one-electron self-interaction, and the adiabatic limit. The paper also contains a mathematical section where we provide a fully rigorous justification of some parts of the text. We particularly discuss the mathematical properties of two operators underlying the two formulations of TDDFT and establish sufficient conditions for their invertibility. We explain the functional-analytic subtleties underlying the geometric interpretation of TDDFT and the two formulations of TDDFT. This unified perspective clarifies the mathematical and conceptual relation between variational and geometric TDDFT and provides a foundation for the development of approximations within geometric TDDFT.

title: Do Embedding-Map Distances Guide LLM Ideation? Four Tests Against What Came Next
abstract: A popular ideation recipe treats an embedding map of existing work as a guide: pick points far from everything and decode them into ideas. I test four ways such distances could guide ideation against what appeared later. (1) Far random directions are not text: no later item reaches a raw cosine above about 0.10 with one (after centring or whitening, 22 of 24 cells stay out of reach), and an LLM decoder shown a target's neighbours, with score-only feedback, writes those neighbours in all six target sets. A neighbour-free search writes coherent text at median cosine 0.57 and 0.47 to interior gaps, beating the nearest existing item on 15 and 14 of 20, but only 0.07 and 0.06 to far points. (2) On k-means cells of a past-only map, the registered hole score mostly tracks cell size and position; three density-based gap scores forecast which cells grow fastest at or below chance (AUC 0.30 to 0.66) and add nothing to momentum in Steam and arXiv, with patents inconclusive; more isolated new Steam games are slightly better reviewed. (3) LLM continuations of arXiv papers stay closer to the source than papers that cite it, under three user prompts and against proposal rewrites (gpt-4o) and April-December 2023 papers (OLMo). Critique lengthens this step beyond content-free revision, replicated on 150 new papers. Revealing a real follow-up's title turns the ideas by 0.032 along a follow-up-specific direction beyond revision; reviewer, oracle and distance feedback add 0.13, 0.08 and 0.34 of that turn (upper bounds 0.46, 0.46, 0.70), and their turn is not separable from revision or their longer step. (4) For inspiration material graded by distance, no inverted U was detected, on an anticipation margin that tracks format more than content. Original tests were registered before running, follow-ups (thirteen requested in two AI-agent reviews) after the main results; all are dated only by local git commits.

title: Atomistic Insights into the All-Optical Switching of GdCo Alloys with Minimal Gd Concentration
abstract: Single-pulse all-optical helicity-independent switching (AO-HIS) is most commonly observed in Gd-based ferrimagnets near magnetization compensation. Recent experiments, however, demonstrated switching in Pt/Co/Pt-based heterostructures containing only a small amount of Gd at a Co/Pt interface. Here, we use atomistic spin-dynamics simulations to test an effective interfacial GdCo-alloy picture and to determine how species-dependent spin-bath coupling controls the minimum Gd concentration required for reversal. We compare a three-monolayer Co film with Gd confined to the surface layer and a three-dimensional uniformly alloyed GdCo model. Within the present uniform-heating model, robust transient toggle-like reversal is obtained far from compensation when the Gd coupling to the thermal bath is substantially weaker than that of Co; for λCo = 0.02 and λCo = 0.001, reversal occurs down to 1.5 at. % total Gd for selected pulse parameters. Increasing the Gd content accelerates reversal, consistent with the interpretation of Gd as an angular-momentum reservoir, whereas dilute interfacial Gd produces slower and more stochastic dynamics. These results show that compensation is not a fundamental requirement for ultrafast AO-HIS and identify the effective Gd spin-bath coupling as a key control parameter. Quantitative comparison with experiment will require explicit optical absorption, stack-dependent heat flow, dipolar fields, and a stable-final-state switching criterion.

title: AISM-REGBF: An Interpretable Regression-Based Framework for Predicting Small- Molecule Potency
abstract: Inflammation is a primary immune response categorized into acute and chronic types, with chronic inflammation linked to various diseases such as autoimmune disorders and cancer. Conventional therapies often face limitations due to side effects and therapeutic resistance, prompting the exploration of small-molecule compounds as safer alternatives. In this study we emphasize the integration of machine learning (ML), particularly through structure-activity relationship (SAR) analysis and quantitative structure-activity relationship (QSAR) modeling, to enhance drug discovery.

title: Planar-Chiral Metal Clusters Direct Polarization-Responsive Supercrystals
abstract: Chiral metal clusters are promising atomically precise building blocks for hierarchical chiral materials, but their programmed assembly into structurally resolved supercrystals with traceable chirality transfer remains challenging. Here, we show that planar-chiral Cu5 clusters can serve as symmetry-defined modules for constructing polarization-responsive supercrystals.
venue: Journal of the American Chemical Society

title: Detecting False Self-Consistency in Density-Functional Calculations
abstract: Density-functional calculations feed materials databases and machine-learning models, and are declared converged when energy changes and residuals fall below thresholds. We show that these criteria, and even the agreement of independent optimizers, can accept a state from which the energy still descends or whose Hamiltonian is inconsistent with the energy. A variational formulation of self-consistency in the space of Kohn-Sham Hamiltonians yields a descent probe that exposes lower states accessible from a returned solution, and a frozen-orbital Janak test detects such an inconsistency. Both apply to any code without modification. In VASP, a UO$_2$ PBE+$U$ calculation converges 1.46 eV above a lower state, and CoO and FeO converge as metals 0.8-0.9 eV above insulating states. In a census of 339 converged calculations on tungsten-free Materials Project structures, recomputed with a modified static protocol, 57 (16.8%) show energy decreases above the threshold, 49 without an initial energy rise exceeding the tolerance.

title: Scaled boundary finite elements for FFT-based computational micromechanics
abstract: We introduce a matrix-free FFT-based solver for three-dimensional linear elastic homogenization problems discretized by the scaled boundary finite element method (SBFEM) on a voxel grid. Owing to its analytical solution in the radial direction, the SBFEM discretization is inherently softer than fully integrated voxel finite elements, whereas its displacement-based formulation remains symmetric, conforming, and supports arbitrary stiffness anisotropy. These properties make SBFEM an attractive candidate for porous and highly heterogeneous microstructures, where existing voxel-based FFT discretizations offer no generally reliable choice: Reduced-integration hexahedral elements, equivalently the rotated staggered grid discretization, may suffer from hourglass instabilities in the presence of voids, whereas fully integrated hexahedral elements are often too stiff. The proposed discretization uses hexahedral SBFEM cells on the full voxel mesh of a regular periodic grid, retaining the simplicity of a fixed-resolution voxel representation without requiring adaptive mesh coarsening. The main contribution is a preconditioner based on the homogeneous SBFEM stiffness operator. We show that this preconditioner may be applied locally in Fourier space and that the condition number of the preconditioned system is bounded by the material contrast, independently of the grid resolution. This result enables a fully matrix-free implementation of the SBFEM-discretized problem, without assembling or storing the global stiffness matrix. Numerical experiments on a short-fibre reinforced composite, a polyurethane foam and a sand-based binder jet microstructure demonstrate robust convergence and competitive accuracy compared with established voxel discretizations. In particular, SBFEM remains stable for porous microstructures, for which reduced-integration hexahedral elements become unstable.

title: Oxirane Ring-Opening Dynamics Mediated By The First Singlet Excitation Using Time-Dependent \textit{GW} Molecular Dynamics
abstract: Oxirane (ethylene oxide, \ce{C2H4O}) is a prototypical system for investigating photoinduced bond cleavage and ring-opening dynamics. Previous time-dependent density functional theory studies identified the initial HOMO $\rightarrow$ LUMO (\ce{S1}) excitation as nonreactive and attributed ring opening to higher-energy excitations. Subsequent constrained density functional theory simulations, however, reported ring opening following an \ce{S2} $\rightarrow$ \ce{S1} transition. Here, we investigate photochemistry of oxirane using time-dependent $GW$ molecular dynamics (TD$GW$-MD), a many-body approach based on extended quasiparticle theory [\textit{J. Chem. Phys.} \textbf{160}, 184102 (2024)]. Our simulations reveal ring opening initiated by asymmetric \ce{C-O} bond cleavage following direct HOMO $\rightarrow$ LUMO (\ce{S1}) excitation. Following the selected surface hop, separate conditional trajectories on the broken-symmetry open-shell singlet and triplet potential energy surfaces lead to distinct products. The singlet trajectory yields acetaldehyde via intramolecular hydrogen transfer, while the triplet trajectory produces formaldehyde and methylene via \ce{C-C} bond fragmentation. These products are consistent with those identified in previous photolysis experiments. Our results demonstrate that direct excitation to the lowest singlet excited state can initiate ring opening within the present TD$GW$-MD framework. They further reveal distinct subsequent reaction pathways under the selected spin conditions. This study highlights the potential of TD$GW$-MD for elucidating photoinduced reaction mechanisms from a many-body perspective.

title: Adsorbate-Free Screening of Dissociative Water Adsorption on Nickel Nanoparticles via Graph Neural Networks
abstract: Dissociative water adsorption is a key step in heterogeneous and electrochemical catalysis, but on finite Ni nanosystems the OH$^*$ and H$^*$ fragments can occupy many combinations of surface sites, making exhaustive density functional theory (DFT) screening impractical. We introduce a graph neural network (GNN) framework with an adsorbate-free representation: candidate O- and H-binding sites are defined by sets of Ni atoms (\textit{anchors}), and each site pair is encoded as a graph constructed solely from these anchors and their local Ni environment. Using only MACE-relaxed bare Ni geometries as input, separate GNNs predict the DFT-reference adsorption energies of OH$^*$+H$^*$ configurations and whether the proposed binding sites would be retained upon DFT relaxation, eliminating the need to construct or relax adsorbates during screening. Trained across Ni nanoclusters and Ni(111)/Ni(100) surfaces, the energy model achieves a mean absolute error of 0.031 eV on the internal validation set and demonstrates transferability to unseen Ni$_{55}$, Ni$_{91}$, and Ni$_{130}$ clusters and larger surface cells, particularly for relative-energy ranking, although quantitative accuracy varies across systems. These independent tests also support the retention classifier's use as a conservative filter for selecting configurations likely to preserve their proposed binding sites. Application to Ni nanoparticles containing up to $\sim$3000 atoms identifies favorable co-adsorption motifs and shows that lower O-site coordination generally stabilizes the dissociated state, whereas H-site coordination has a weaker influence. The framework thus offers an efficient route to screening adsorption energetics, with potential extensions to other metals and adsorbate combinations.

title: Kinetic and Thermodynamic Limits of Sodium Pore Filling in Hard Carbon
abstract: The low-voltage plateau-like capacity of hard carbon anodes is widely regarded as a key signature of sodium storage in closed pores, often defining the performance of Na-ion batteries. Here, we combine first-principles calculations with a grand canonical Monte Carlo pore-filling model to show that Na storage in closed pores is not governed by a single equilibrium-plateau mechanism but by a distribution of pore-specific thermodynamic and kinetic activation processes. Thermodynamically, the voltage at which Na pore filling becomes favorable decreases with increasing pore size. Kinetically, pore filling involves Na nucleation, coalescence, growth, and bulk diffusion. While small pores fill rapidly, large pores exhibit both a smaller thermodynamic stimulus and significant kinetic limitations. Nucleation can be accelerated by introducing defects at the pore walls, although an excessively high defect concentration slows bulk diffusion. This work shows that not all closed pores contribute equally to Na storage: some may be thermodynamically favorable but kinetically inactive under realistic charge/discharge rates. Because of this, the inverse design of hard carbon electrodes should target a kinetically accessible pore-size and defect-density window that balances high plateau-like capacity with fast-charging performance.

title: Reduced Density Matrices from Renormalization-Group Flows
abstract: We reconstruct complete one- and two-body reduced density matrices (RDMs) by a single collective backward evolution along the in-medium similarity renormalization-group flow. Benchmarks show improved accuracy and physical consistency over conventional elementwise evolution. In neutron matter, two-body RDMs reveal spin-triplet dominance in interaction-dependent Fermi-sea depletion trends. Meanwhile, the forward-backward energy difference provides an internal diagnostic of many-body truncation errors, whose quantification remains challenging in nuclear $ab\ initio$ calculations.

title: Cavity Control of Emission Dynamics from Spin Defects in Hexagonal Boron Nitride
abstract: Optically addressable negatively charged boron vacancy ($\mathrm{V_B^-}$) defects in hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) are promising for quantum sensing at room temperature. The two-dimensional structure of hBN allows direct access to the local environment, enabling proximal sensing of target materials. However, its broadband emission and low quantum yield hinder efficient light-matter interaction, and the coupling of $\mathrm{V_B^-}$ optical dipoles to confined cavity fields remains poorly understood. In this study, we integrate $\mathrm{V_B^-}$ defects with a tunable plano-concave microcavity, achieving three-dimensional optical confinement. This approach yields photoluminescence (PL) enhancement and cavity-modified optical decay dynamics, providing insights into the orientation of the $\mathrm{V_B^-}$ defect dipole. Time-resolved PL measurements identify a distinct fast decay component, suggesting a complex dipole geometry for the defects. Therefore, a tilted optical dipole model is considered to attribute the fast and slow decay components to in-plane and out-of-plane dipole contributions, respectively. Additionally, optically detected magnetic resonance and excitation-polarisation-dependent PL measurements provide further insights into local symmetry breaking and potential optical dipole configurations. These results highlight the role of optical dipole orientation in $\mathrm{V_B^-}$ defect-cavity coupling.

title: Integrated Network Toxicology, Machine Learning, and Structural Biology Identify a Candidate Gene Network Linking Predicted Acetyl Tributyl Citrate Targets to Alzheimer's Disease.
abstract: As a common plasticizer, acetyl tributyl citrate (ATBC) poses a potential public health risk, yet its role in Alzheimer's disease (AD) is unclear. This study seeks to identify candidate molecular links between computationally predicted ATBC targets and AD-associated transcriptional alterations. We combined differential gene expression and co-expression results from two AD-related transcriptomic datasets with in silico ATBC target predictions from ChEMBL, PharmMapper, and SwissTargetPrediction, followed by machine learning feature selection, network toxicology, and molecular docking.

title: Cardiomyocytes in Persistent Cancer Therapy-related Cardiac Dysfunction Show Contractile and Natriuretic Peptide Signaling Signatures
abstract: BACKGROUND. Anthracycline and trastuzumab therapy of HER2-positive breast cancer causes cancer therapy-related cardiac dysfunction (CTRCD) in a subset of treated patients. Some recover cardiac function, others do not. Whether persistence is a cardiomyocyte-intrinsic property is unknown. OBJECTIVES. We sought to determine whether induced pluripotent stem cell-derived cardiomyocytes (iPSC-CMs) from patients with persistent CTRCD respond to these drugs differently from those of patients with reversible or no CTRCD, and to identify the functional pathways involved. METHODS. iPSCs were derived from 23 women with normal baseline cardiac function treated with doxorubicin-based chemotherapy followed by trastuzumab: 5, 11 and 7 with no, reversible, and persistent CTRCD, respectively. iPSC-CMs were exposed to 7 drug regimens, generating 161 transcriptomic profiles that we resolved by singular value decomposition and subjected to pathway enrichment analysis. Reliability was tested by 100 clinical label permutations and leave-one-patient-out downsampling. RESULTS. Persistent CTRCD responses clustered more tightly and separated from reversible and no-CTRCD responses to a higher degree than expected by chance (P = 0.04). Reversible and no-CTRCD responses did not resolve from one another. Genes encoding guideline-recommended biomarkers, including natriuretic peptides and cardiac troponins, were more strongly induced or less repressed in persistent CTRCD cell lines, while natriuretic peptide receptor signaling was lower. Contraction, calcium handling, cytoskeletal and glycolytic pathways differed between CTRCD groups. Comparison with signatures induced by cardiotoxic kinase inhibitors in healthy donor cardiomyocytes documented high functional similarities. CONCLUSIONS. Cardiomyocytes display a cell-intrinsic signature of persistent CTRCD that centers on contractile homeostasis and natriuretic peptide receptor signaling, supporting patient group-selective cardioprotective intervention strategies.

title: AI-supported screening for systematic literature reviews informing EULAR recommendations and points to consider
abstract: ObjectivesThis study aims to improve the efficiency of title and abstract screening in systematic literature reviews (SLRs) supporting European Alliance of Associations for Rheumatology (EULAR) recommendations and points to consider, by developing and validating stopping criteria for active learning-assisted screening that achieve ≥95% recall (ie, sensitivity).MethodsSimulation studies analysed 40 development and 5 validation datasets (202,177 records) from completed and ongoing EULAR SLRs, using active learning models (h3, u3, and u4) in ASReview. Time-to-event analyses estimated the proportion of records that required screening to reach 95% recall and the minimum safe streak length (longest sequence of irrelevant records before reaching 95% recall). Empirical stopping criteria were derived, tested on independent datasets and evaluated for workload reduction and time savings.ResultsDatasets averaged 4493 records (SD, 2851), with a mean of 67 (SD, 46) records included. The u4 model was optimal for balancing screening efficacy and computational efficiency. Target recall was achieved after screening 35% of records or reaching sequences of 15% nonrelevant records. A combined criterion (26% screened plus 10% irrelevant streak) provided an alternative stopping criterion. Validation met target recall. Screening workload was reduced by 67.1%.ConclusionsEmpirically derived stopping criteria using an active learning tool can substantially accelerate SLR screening while maintaining high recall (≥95%), allowing reviewers to skip about two-thirds of records during title and abstract screening. Artificial intelligence-assisted screening can substantially reduce evidence synthesis workload, thus supporting more efficient development of EULAR recommendations and points to consider.

title: SciResearch-Eval: Evaluating Scientific Judgment in Autonomous Experimental Agents
abstract: We introduce SciResearch-Eval, an interactive benchmark of scientific judgment built on a standard laboratory problem: measuring a material's thermal properties by heating it and fitting a heat-conduction simulator. An agent designs its own experiments, uses a supplied simulator that may be under-resolved or physically wrong, and reports each property with a 95% interval. To our knowledge it is the first benchmark to combine agent-designed experiments, a deliberately flawed simulator, and proper scoring of calibrated intervals against exact ground truth. On a held-out split (93 tasks, 9 models, 2,511 episodes), models handle procedural traps. When the simulator is missing physics, most report wrong values while stating they are 95% sure: their ranges contain the truth in 20-62% of cases, against 94% for GPT-6 Astra and 99% for Claude Fable 5.2. At default effort the failing Claude 5.5 models rarely diagnose the missing physics (Opus in 35% of episodes, against 66% for Astra), and even when they do, their ranges often miss; Astra and Fable design experiments in which the flawed simulator is accurate, such as gentle heating, which keeps Astra calibrated even when it does not name the cause. Asking for wider intervals does not help; stating the strategy improves interval scores 1.6-2.5-fold, replicated on a pre-registered fresh split, but coverage barely moves. A pre-registered effort ablation shows that the correction is latent in the Claude 5.5 models: at maximum effort Opus improves more than tenfold and is no longer detectably behind Astra at default, but only with 13-31 times more reasoning; older and open-weight models gain nothing. Fable 5.2 is the most accurate model at default effort (interval score 1.9 times better than Astra's) but writes 6 times as many tokens, and at Astra's token count it falls short. We release the environment, graders and harness.

title: ScenarioForge: Resource-Grounded Generation and Execution Validation of Cyber Exercises
abstract: Cyber-range and capture-the-flag scenario construction remains labor-intensive because authors must coordinate infrastructure, vulnerable services, attack paths, artifacts, and success conditions. LLMs can propose detailed exercises, but plausible descriptions do not guarantee deployable software or verifiable objectives. We present ScenarioForge, which turns high-level requirements into resource-grounded topologies, services, traffic, segmentation, and challenge chains, then instantiates and validates them in the Common Open Research Emulator (CORE). The ScenarioForge Execution Dataset contains 226 materialized scenarios covering 294 Vulhub images and all 85 custom-built challenge-resource generators developed with our AI-assisted scaffolding. All 226 passed construction, preview, sequencing, deployment, strict runtime validation, and live artifact checks; their 867 steps, each an individually verifiable challenge objective, comprise 457 vulnerability-backed and 410 generated-resource-backed instances. In a separate 50-prompt matched benchmark, ScenarioForge+Qwen3.8 and ScenarioForge+GPT5.6 each achieved 50/50 (100%) topology/build success and 160/160 intent fields; direct frontier generation reached 41/50 builds and 147/160 fields only with the full cumulative scaffold: structure, vocabulary, policy, and container-image guidance. The test still omitted ScenarioForge's downstream challenge-resource generation, dependency/flag sequencing, deployment, and live validation. The artifacts support operationally rich, reproducible exercises for training and evaluation.

title: K 2 Mn 2 ( MoO 4 ) 3 : Coupled Fluctuations and Magnetic Phase Diagram
abstract: Structure−property relationships of K2Mn2(MoO4)3 are investigated by X-ray diffraction, Raman spectroscopy, and thermodynamic property measurements. The compound crystallizes in the acentric, polar space group Pba2 which allows for magnetoelastic coupling of the lattice to spin fluctuations. Experimental evidence for a pseudo-Peierls distortion is discussed and supported by two-endmember decomposition and principal component analysis of temperature-dependent Raman spectroscopic data. The simulation of the susceptibility data above the antiferromagnetic long-range ordering (LRO) temperature is based on a quasi-1D chain model, relating to super-superexchange (SSE) via molybdate bridging units for Mn1 and a perpendicularly orientated sawtooth chain (Mn2,3) with super-exchange (SE) pathways. The magnetic phase diagram is presented for K2Mn2(MoO4)3 with three magnetic transition temperatures in zero applied magnetic fields. Interestingly, a rather extended regime of short-range order (SRO) exists. This is assigned to a decoupling of magnetic LRO towards 1D characteristics. K2Mn2(MoO4)3 belongs to the class of materials with competing interactions as indicated by the so-called frustration parameter f = |ΘCW/TN| = 7.1.
